title: Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel
desc: Contrasts contextual tests for corrected neglect, balancing client protection, judicial discretion and consistent procedural enforcement.

kps.k: Delegation and software reliance do not eliminate lawyer responsibility, but resulting errors need not automatically forfeit a client's case.
kps.d: Pincay and Taylor distinguish professional care from procedural relief after a missed deadline. Pincay recognizes the cost advantages and possible accuracy benefits of delegating repetitive work, while faulting counsel for failing to check the governing rule. Taylor requires a factual inquiry into whether reasonably prudent counsel could have experienced the alleged docketing-software failure. These cases concern paralegals and conventional software, not AI; their relevance to AI reliance is analogical rather than a direct holding.

kps.k: Both majorities require contextual consideration, but apply different tests and reach different procedural outcomes.
kps.d: Pincay applies Pioneer's four factors: prejudice, delay and procedural impact, the reason for delay and its controllability, and good faith. It upholds an appeal extension after a paralegal confused a 30-day deadline with a 60-day deadline, given the short delay, lack of prejudice and absence of bad faith. Taylor applies Colorado's Craig inquiry into excusable neglect, a meritorious claim or defense, and equity. It remands for reconsideration of a non-merits dismissal rather than finding the malfunction excusable or ordering reinstatement. Neither decision establishes an automatic entitlement to relief.

qs.q: The _Pioneer_ factors include: (1) the danger of prejudice to the non-moving party, (2) the length of delay and its potential impact on judicial proceedings, (3) the reason for the delay, including whether it was within the reasonable control of the movant, and (4) whether the moving party's conduct was in good faith.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

kps.k: The central disagreement concerns whether harmless, promptly corrected neglect still needs an affirmative justification.
kps.d: In Pincay, Berzon treats excusability as the outcome of equitable balancing: even a professionally unacceptable mistake may warrant relief if genuine, quickly caught and harmless. Kozinski's dissent gives the reason for delay central weight and finds no justification in a system that accurately recorded a legally incorrect deadline. He warns that leniency could encourage deficient delegation; this is an incentive prediction, not empirical evidence. In Taylor, Berger instead emphasizes that computer failures can occur despite reasonable care and considers counsel's uncontradicted account sufficient. The majority leaves that assessment unresolved.

qs.q: _Pioneer_ thus indicates that a district court may find neglect "excusable" if it is caught quickly, hurts no one, and is a real mistake, rather than one feigned for some tactical reason — _even if_ no decent lawyer would have made that error.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

qs.q: Given the ubiquitous use of computers in law practice and every other aspect of modern life, courts should adjust to the reality that computer failures happen despite a user's reasonable care.
qs.a: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943 · Regulators & courts · 2018

kps.k: Judicial discretion creates a separate tension between individualized justice and consistent enforcement.
kps.d: Pincay's majority favors trial-court judgment and acknowledges that denying the extension might also have survived appellate review. Kozinski argues that excessive deference weakens meaningful review and produces judge-dependent outcomes; the opinions also describe conflicting circuit interpretations of Pioneer. Taylor likewise assigns the initial factual assessment to the trial court, but holds that applying the wrong legal test constitutes an abuse of discretion. The shared emphasis on context therefore does not remove appellate constraints or establish a uniform rule across jurisdictions.

qs.q: Had the district court declined to permit the filing of the notice, we would be hard pressed to find any rationale requiring us to reverse.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

qs.q: Here, the district court failed to resolve Taylor's motion in accordance with the applicable legal standard.
qs.a: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943 · Regulators & courts · 2018

kps.k: Client protection supplies a rationale for relief distinct from excusing counsel's conduct.
kps.d: Berger's separate Taylor opinion would require reinstatement when counsel alone bears fault, the client has a meritorious claim and defendants face no legal prejudice. He would generally deny relief where serious prejudice accompanies client blameworthiness. He also rejects assuming that malpractice litigation adequately replaces the lost case, pointing to the burdens of proving a case within a case and possible collectability. These are proposed doctrinal reforms, not the majority's holding; his assessment of Taylor's claim expressly precedes adversarial testing.

qs.q: ¶ 93 In those cases in which the fault lies entirely with the lawyer, the plaintiff has a meritorious cause of action, and the defendants will not suffer any legal prejudice if the default judgment or dismissal is vacated, I would conclude that it would be an abuse of discretion not to reinstate the case.
qs.a: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943 · Regulators & courts · 2018

qs.q: ¶ 94 On the other hand, when the defendants will suffer serious prejudice by reinstatement of the case and the plaintiff herself is blameworthy, it will generally be an abuse of discretion to set aside the judgment.
qs.a: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943 · Regulators & courts · 2018

kps.k: The practical implications center on checking critical deadlines, documenting failures and seeking relief promptly.
kps.d: Pincay underscores that delegating calendaring does not replace counsel's duty to check the applicable rule. Taylor shows why a specific account of the malfunction and supporting records matter, without treating counsel's explanation as conclusively established. Prompt action strengthens the equitable case: Pincay involved an application within the limited extension window, and Taylor sought relief on the dismissal date. Taylor also permits further evidence at the contemplated hearing, reconciling prompt filing with investigation. Relief remains subject to the applicable procedural regime, evidence of merit where required, and prejudice to the opposing party.

qs.q: Andrews's counsel learned about the error when Pincay relied upon the judgment as being final in related bankruptcy proceedings, and Andrews promptly tendered a notice of appeal together with a request for an extension within the 30-day grace period.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

qs.q: An exhibit to the motion appeared to show that counsel had not received an electronic notification of the delay reduction order from the court's filing system on her computer, and another exhibit confirmed that the delay reduction order had not been opened by counsel.
qs.a: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943 · Regulators & courts · 2018

vlens.an: These selected judicial sources support the proposition that delegation or software reliance leaves counsel professionally responsible, while client forfeiture should be assessed separately under the applicable contextual relief standard. Both majorities reject automatic rules: Pincay upholds discretionary relief despite an egregious delegated error, whereas Taylor remands for factual and equitable analysis without deciding that the software malfunction was excusable. Their common reasoning emphasizes prejudice, prompt correction, good faith or equity, and trial-court assessment rather than treating either counsel’s fault or technological involvement as dispositive. Material variation concerns how demanding relief should be. Pincay’s majority and Berzon permit relief even for professionally unacceptable mistakes when the broader balance favors it; Kozinski’s dissent insists on an affirmative justification and warns that leniency may weaken competence and consistency. In Taylor, the majority remains procedurally cautious, while Berger would go further by protecting a blameless client with a meritorious claim whenever defendants would suffer no legal prejudice. These decisions concern paralegal delegation and conventional docketing software, so any application to AI is analogical, not a direct judicial holding.

qs.q: In this case the mistake itself, the misreading of the Rule, was egregious, and the lawyer undoubtedly should have checked the Rule itself before relying on the paralegal's reading.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

qs.q: ¶ 93 In those cases in which the fault lies entirely with the lawyer, the plaintiff has a meritorious cause of action, and the defendants will not suffer any legal prejudice if the default judgment or dismissal is vacated, I would conclude that it would be an abuse of discretion not to reinstate the case.

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition that delegation does not displace lawyer responsibility, while a delegated error need not automatically forfeit the client’s case. Pincay treats paralegal delegation as a practical and potentially accuracy-enhancing feature of legal practice, but still characterizes counsel’s failure to verify the governing deadline as egregious. The majority nevertheless rejects a categorical rule of forfeiture and permits relief through contextual equitable balancing, particularly where delay is short, prejudice and bad faith are absent, and the error is promptly addressed. Material internal variation concerns the threshold for relief and the scope of judicial discretion: Berzon’s concurrence separates professional unacceptability from procedural excusability, whereas Kozinski’s dissent insists that even harmless neglect needs an affirmative justification and warns that leniency may weaken competence incentives and consistent appellate enforcement. Thus, the decision supports the proposition overall while exposing its central tensions. Its relevance to AI is analogical because it concerns a paralegal rather than an AI system.

qs.q: In this case the mistake itself, the misreading of the Rule, was egregious, and the lawyer undoubtedly should have checked the Rule itself before relying on the paralegal's reading.

qs.q: We now hold that per se rules are not consistent with _Pioneer,_ and we uphold the exercise of the district court's discretion to permit the filing of the notice of appeal in this case.
qs.a: Pincay v. Andrews, 389 F.3d 853 (9th Cir. 2004) (en banc) · Regulators & courts · 2004

elens.an: The sole supplied source for 2015–2022 supports the proposition that reliance on delegated technology does not automatically excuse counsel, while procedural relief may still protect a client from forfeiture. Taylor’s majority treats the docketing-software failure as a fact-specific question of reasonable prudence and requires application of the full Craig test—excusable neglect, merits and equity—rather than either automatically excusing the malfunction or treating counsel’s error as dispositive. It therefore remands for reconsideration without deciding whether relief must be granted. Material internal variation appears in Judge Berger’s separate opinion: he would go further by finding the computer-related neglect excusable on the record and requiring reinstatement where fault lies entirely with counsel, the client has a meritorious claim and defendants face no legal prejudice. Thus, the opinions agree on contextual assessment and the possibility of client relief, but differ over whether the existing record justifies immediate relief and whether client innocence and lack of prejudice should support a stronger doctrinal rule. Because this is one curated judicial source concerning conventional docketing software rather than AI, it supplies an analogy rather than evidence of a broader period-wide consensus about AI automation.
